candidates.attacker_control: The `redirectedFrom` POST parameter is fully attacker-controlled (sent in the request body/query of a POST to /module/appointmentscheduling/appointmentBlockForm). A crafted POST containing e.g. `emptyTypes=no&redirectedFrom=https://attacker.example` follows a path with no action/void/purge/save/unvoid parameter and reaches the redirect sink. No CSRF token is present on this legacy form, so a third-party page can auto-submit the request to the trusted OpenMRS host.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Searched all Java sources for `redirectedFrom`, `redirect:`, and `sendRedirect`: the only dynamic redirect target in the repository is line 313 (every other redirect value is a constant view/URL). Confirmed the parameter is not validated at the sink and that the GET handler's equality check is not security-relevant to the POST path. Confirmed the sink line lies outside the Context.isAuthenticated() block (line 162 opens, line 312 closes). Verified Spring semantics from framework conventions: UrlBasedViewResolver.createView handles the `redirect:` prefix before resource/view checks, and RedirectView prepends the context path only when the URL starts with "/", so absolute URLs escape. No test or runtime confirmation was performed.
candidates.impact: A trusted OpenMRS host can be used as a redirector to arbitrary external sites (phishing/credential-harvesting pages that mimic the OpenMRS login, malware delivery, or bypassing URL-based trust). Combined with the absence of CSRF protection on the legacy form, the redirect can be triggered from a page the victim merely visits, without the victim intentionally submitting the form.
candidates.prerequisites: A victim request that reaches the controller, in practice an authenticated OpenMRS session (the sink at line 313 executes outside the Context.isAuthenticated() block, so it also runs for a request that reaches the controller unauthenticated, but OpenMRS core's web filter may redirect anonymous users to login first). `emptyTypes` must be non-null to avoid an NPE at line 163 before the sink. The supplied target must be an absolute URL (leading "/" is prefixed with the context path by Spring's context-relative RedirectView default, whereas `https://...` is passed through).
candidates.root_cause: AppointmentBlockFormController.onSubmit accepts the request parameter `redirectedFrom` (line 157) and uses it directly to build the Spring view name `"redirect:" + redirectedFrom` at line 313, with no whitelist or validation. Spring's UrlBasedViewResolver treats a name with the `redirect:` prefix as a RedirectView, so an absolute value such as `https://attacker.example` becomes a Location header. The GET handler (lines 79-95) only compares `redirectedFrom` to the literal "appointmentBlockCalendar.list" for prefill logic and then stores the raw value in the model; no allow-list is enforced at the redirect sink, and no other control in the module sanitizes the parameter.
candidates.title: Open redirect via unvalidated `redirectedFrom` parameter in AppointmentBlockFormController
candidates.trace: HTTP POST /module/appointmentscheduling/appointmentBlockForm -> @RequestParam("redirectedFrom") String redirectedFrom (line 157) -> no matching action branch (lines 169/201/221/306) -> line 312 closes the authenticated block -> line 313 `return "redirect:" + redirectedFrom;` -> UrlBasedViewResolver recognizes the `redirect:` prefix and creates a RedirectView with the attacker-supplied URL -> HTTP 302 Location: https://attacker.example.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed; Spring view-resolver configuration inside the deployed OpenMRS webapp (e.g. redirectContextRelative / resolver chain) and OpenMRS core filter behavior for this .form URL were inferred from framework conventions and cannot be verified from this snapshot. Whether upstream intended a whitelist here is unknown; alternate code paths (save/void/purge/unvoid) return earlier and were not part of the taint path. The module's JSP views live in another repository, so no server-side rendering behavior could be checked.
candidates.weakness_type: Open Redirect / URL Redirection to Untrusted Site (CWE-601)

coverage_summary: Scope: 189 source files (parity statement: same filters for B0/P1; 0 files excluded for size, sensitive names, or symlinks; binary-like files skipped by the readers; 189/189 files indexed by the relation index with 1150 symbols, 2955 calls, 1766 edges, 103 facts, no SAST/data-flow loaded). Reviewed the api module (entities, DAO interfaces and Hibernate DAOs, AppointmentServiceImpl, validators, reporting query/data evaluators, tasks, activator), the omod (all web controllers, REST resources and search handler, DWRAppointmentService, editors, extensions, config.xml, web/module spring contexts), and the hbm/liquibase/pom resources. Extensive grep/trace search was used for authorization annotations, query construction, redirects, and injection sinks; all createQuery/createSQLQuery call sites were inspected. Not reviewed line-by-line: third-party bundled JavaScript/CSS (jQuery, fullCalendar, jqPlot, TableTools, ZeroClipboard, json2, jquery-ui, dataTables).
limitations: No code execution, tests, scanners, or runtime confirmation; all conclusions are static source analysis.

OpenMRS core behavior (OpenmrsFilter authentication for /dwr and module .form URLs, enforcement of @Authorized via serviceInterceptors, and the deployed Spring view resolver configuration) is outside the snapshot and was assumed from framework conventions.
Module view JSPs are not in this snapshot (they live in a separate UI module), so output-encoding/XSS and redirect rendering behavior could not be verified.
The relation index is syntactic only; unresolved call sites and reflection/AOP behavior may hide some data flow.
Third-party JavaScript libraries were not reviewed in depth.

rejected_leads.lead: Missing privilege requirements on several AppointmentService methods: bare @Authorized on createTimeSlotUsingProviderSchedule/getTimeslotForAppointment (AppointmentService.java:1113-1117), getProviderScheduleByUuid (:1064), getAllProviderSchedules() (:1034) while sibling methods require View/Manage Provider Schedules. AppointmentRequisitionController (POST /rest/v1/appointmentscheduling/createappointment) reaches createTimeSlotUsingProviderSchedule and can persist AppointmentBlocks/TimeSlots as any authenticated user, and ProviderScheduleResource1_9.getByUniqueId exposes provider schedules without the View Provider Schedules privilege.
rejected_leads.reason: Real authorization inconsistency but most likely inherited upstream design (bare @Authorized means 'any authenticated user'); it requires an authenticated account, the write occurs as a side effect with the booking itself still gated by Schedule Appointments, and intent cannot be established from this snapshot, so it is weaker than the concrete tainted-sink finding.

rejected_leads.lead: DWRAppointmentService.getPatientDescription (omod/.../web/DWRAppointmentService.java:39-61) is the only DWR method lacking a Context.isAuthenticated() guard, and its DWR include is registered in config.xml.
rejected_leads.reason: No demonstrated data exposure: the method calls core PatientService.getPatient, AppointmentService.getLastAppointment and getPatientIdentifiersRepresentation, which are annotated @Authorized in core/module and would fail for anonymous callers; DWR reachability without a session depends on OpenMRS core webapp filters outside this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: The 'Task: appointmentschedulingui.viewConfidential' privilege (AppointmentSchedulingConstants, config.xml) is only enforced in PatientToAppointmentDataEvaluator/PersonToAppointmentDataEvaluator; AppointmentPropertyDataEvaluator and the REST AppointmentResource1_9 expose appointment/patient details without checking it.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible confidentiality-control gap, but 'confidential' semantics and the intended enforcement point are ambiguous from this snapshot (the UI module that consumes these APIs is out of scope), so it does not meet the evidence threshold as a single distinct finding.

rejected_leads.lead: AppointmentSettingsFormController.onSubmit persists global properties without checking the module's 'Manage Appointments Settings' privilege; PatientDashboardAppointmentExtController changes appointment status via saveAppointment without the 'Update Appointment Status' privilege and without writing AppointmentStatusHistory.
rejected_leads.reason: Underlying core/service calls are themselves privileged (Manage Global Properties / Schedule Appointments), so these are privilege-model and audit-trail inconsistencies rather than demonstrated bypasses.

rejected_leads.lead: HibernateAppointmentDAO.getAppointmentDailyCount uses a native SQL query with positional parameters whose indices shift when fromDate/toDate are null, and HibernateProviderScheduleDAO prints stack traces; AppointmentBlockListController can NPE on missing date parameters.
rejected_leads.reason: Robustness/functional defects without a security impact (the SQL is parameterized, so no injection).

summary: Reviewed the 189-file OpenMRS Appointment Scheduling module snapshot (api + omod, config/hbm/liquibase, REST resources, legacy web controllers, DWR service) using text search and the syntactic relation index. The strongest source-evidenced issue is an unvalidated redirect in AppointmentBlockFormController.onSubmit: the request parameter `redirectedFrom` is bound with @RequestParam and then concatenated verbatim into a Spring redirect view name ("redirect:" + redirectedFrom), producing an attacker-controlled 302 to an arbitrary absolute URL (open redirect). It is the only dynamic redirect sink in the Java sources (all other redirect targets are constants), and the GET handler only equality-checks one value for feature logic while still propagating any value into the model. Other suspicious areas (bare @Authorized on provider-schedule/requisition service methods, missing Context.isAuthenticated() in one DWR method, non-enforcement of the confidential-appointment privilege in REST) were examined and are weaker or ambiguous; they are listed as rejected leads.
